instructions.task: Which question-generation mode best fits the TARGET ARTICLE: fact_pattern, lookup, or skip? Select one mode; do not generate questions or answers.

input_structure.### TARGET ARTICLE: The article whose legal rule questions must concern.
input_structure.### REFERENCED ARTICLES: Cited provisions from the same act.

instructions.metadata: Blocks include a language tag, article number and title, an Act line identifying the instrument and subject matter, and sometimes a Location. Other-act references and all annexes carry a Cite as key. Empty blocks are marked. Different-language versions represent the same provision.
instructions.grounding: The target must supply the legal point. References may complete its rule, but must not become the question's real subject. Metadata identifies the regime, not an answer. A missing reference excludes only questions that depend on its content.
selection: Choose fact_pattern when a concrete situation with at least two legally relevant particulars naturally instantiates the target's conditions. A fictional actor or location added to a general request is not enough.
Choose lookup when the useful information need is a direct point of law and adding a case would mainly decorate it or require unsupported assumptions.

Both modes can ask about scope, definitions, obligations, conditions, deadlines, amounts, procedures, and consequences. A number, definition, formal addressee, or act identifier does not determine the mode.
Use the strongest substantive opportunity in a mixed article; one useful question is enough. Skip boilerplate-only or unsupported content, not an article merely because one clause is unusable.
Both modes need enough actor, product, activity, or legal-term specificity to identify the regime without an act identifier. Follow the distinctions illustrated below, not the example frequencies.
instructions.examples_note: These are illustrative excerpts from the supplied EUR-Lex generation prompts, not scored Jev errors or independently verified legislative quotations. Ellipses indicate omitted source wording.

input.metadata: Article 98 — Decisions of the jury; utilities procurement directive.
input.target_excerpt: The jury shall examine the plans and projects submitted by the candidates anonymously and solely on the basis of the criteria indicated in the contest notice.

examples.reason: A water utility running a design contest and a jury considering unannounced criteria form a concrete case directly decided by the rule. The utility and contest details identify the regime; they are not decorative facts.

input.metadata: Article 10 of Commission Directive 2010/43/EU; organisational requirements for UCITS management companies.
input.target_excerpt: a compliance officer must be appointed and must be responsible for … reporting on a frequent basis, and at least annually, to the senior management on matters of compliance …

examples.reason: The natural need is the reporting frequency for a UCITS management company's compliance officer. A made-up company and country would add little to that direct point of law. Keep the UCITS regime anchor.

input.metadata: Article 1 of the Euratom regulation exempting small quantities of ores, source materials and special fissile materials from the Treaty's chapter on supplies.
input.target_excerpt: transfers within and imports into the Community of quantities not exceeding, per transaction a dosage of one tonne of uranium and thorium (or uranium or thorium), within a limit of five tonnes per year per user in respect of each of these materials

examples.reason: The per-transaction and annual quantities can both be instantiated in a concrete import case within the stated limits. These particulars decide the exemption question, so the case adds substance rather than merely decorating a threshold lookup.

input.metadata: Article 9 — Advisory body; Commission Regulation (EU) No 1300/2014, accessibility of the rail system for persons with reduced mobility.
input.target_excerpt: The tasks of the advisory body shall include: (a) monitoring the development of a minimum data structure for the inventory of assets, …

examples.reason: The target assigns a specific technical task to a body in the rail-accessibility regime. Identifying that body or task is a useful direct legal lookup; the excerpt supplies no natural private-party case with two rule-relevant particulars.

input.metadata: Article 2 of Commission Directive 2012/4/EU; transposition clause.
input.target_excerpt: Member States shall adopt and publish, by 4 April 2012 at the latest, the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive …

examples.reason: This is a transposition clause, not a substantive client-facing requirement. Its exact date and instrument identifier do not turn excluded boilerplate into a suitable lookup or fact pattern.

criteria.fact_pattern: A practitioner describes a concrete private-party situation or a national authority's file without naming the governing instrument. At least two legally relevant particulars instantiate conditions the target explicitly addresses. The question asks how the rule treats the case: applicability, permission, obligation, prerequisite, deadline, amount, procedure, or consequence. The facts do not give away the answer; no unsupported legal reasoning is needed.
criteria.lookup: A practitioner knows the legal regime and wants one point of law: a definition, scope rule, obligation, condition, deadline, threshold, reporting duty, consequence, competent body, or procedure. A specific regime anchor makes the question self-contained. Two renderings differ only by insertion of the target act's identifier; a concrete client situation is unnecessary.
criteria.skip: Neither mode supports a substantive, informative, grounded question about the target. This includes boilerplate such as transposition, general entry into force, repeal, generic institutional review or generic penalties, and cases where indispensable answer substance is missing.
